abstract: Cochlear synaptopathy (CS) can occur during normal aging without elevated audiometric thresholds and has been hypothesized to contribute to suprathreshold auditory difficulties. Frequency-following responses (FFRs) have been proposed as markers of CS, but whether their envelope- and temporal-fine-structure-related components are similarly affected by age, and whether such changes relate to perceptual sensitivity, remains unclear. Here, we examined associations between age-related FFR changes and perceptual sensitivity in young (n = 20, 19-32 years) and middle-aged (n = 20, 40-58 years) adults with clinically normal hearing. Participants completed psychoacoustic discrimination tasks for formant frequency, formant bandwidth, and temporal-envelope shape using stationary stimuli in quiet and background noise. FFRs were recorded using dynamic stimuli varying along the same acoustic dimensions. We quantified envelope- and temporal-fine-structure-related phase locking (PLVENV and PLVTFS) across harmonics and assessed how it tracked stimulus changes over time. Mean PLVENV decreased significantly with age, and PLVENV tracking of decreasing formant bandwidth and temporal-envelope shape weakened with age. In contrast, mean PLVTFS and temporal slopes of PLVTFS spectral centroid were not significantly associated with age. Discrimination thresholds showed no significant associations with age, either in quiet or in noise, and PLV measures did not significantly explain individual differences in discrimination thresholds. These findings indicate that age-related reductions in subcortical envelope phase locking can be detected by middle age without corresponding measurable reductions in perceptual sensitivity.
